title: Following the TRAIL: Evaluation of a Common Typographical Error in Healthcare Literature
content: Background: Typographical errors in healthcare literature are common. Those that involve the use of correctly spelled but contextually inappropriate words are particularly troublesome. Objectives: To estimate the number of uses of the word ‘trail’ in healthcare literature that represent typographical errors. Design: Study design based upon systematic review methodology.Search strategy: The search was designed to identify all uses of the word ‘trail’, then exclude those where use was intentional. Data sources: Six electronic databases were searched from inception to 19th May, 2025.Sampling: 374 of the 14,066 identified records were reviewed, enabling the total number of typographical errors to be estimated with a 5% margin of error and a 95% confidence level. Data extraction and synthesis: Two reviewers independently determined whether the use of the word ‘trail’ was a typographical error. Results: 245 of 374 reviewed records (65.5%, 95% exact binomial CI: 60.4% to 70.3%) contained an inappropriate use of the word ‘trail’. Extrapolating this proportion to all identified records suggests that approximately 9,214 uses of the word ‘trail’ are erroneous (95% CI: 8,502 to 9,891).The majority were misspellings of the word ‘trial’ (e.g. ‘randomised controlled trail’), but other intended words included ‘tail’ and ‘frail’. One particularly enjoyable error involved the use of ‘trail splantati’ in place of ‘transplantation’. Errors were found in peer-reviewed journal publications, protocol registrations and trial registrations. Most errors were in the abstract (63%) or title (24%). Conclusions: Authors frequently write ‘trail’ when they mean ‘trial’. A potential solution is presented in the manuscript.
